rationale: I'm replacing the Fisher-z Pearson features with a tangent-space embedding of Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage covariances. This was the strongest classic pipeline on ABIDE (Abraham 2017). Each subject's matrix is projected at the Riemannian mean of the training fold, which accounts for the geometry of covariance matrices and removes the shared connectivity structure. Shrinkage keeps the short scans (fewer timepoints than ROIs) and all-zero ROIs well-conditioned. I haven't run it, so there is no Dev score for it yet; the current best is 0.736615.

Site effects in ABIDE are large (scanner, sequence, TR), and they show up as a site-specific shift on the SPD manifold. I'm adding Riemannian re-centering: each subject's covariance is whitened by its own site's geometric mean, C → M_site^{-1/2} C M_site^{-1/2}. The site means are computed from all of that site's subjects in train and test, using covariances only and never labels. This puts every site at the identity before the tangent-space projection. In transfer-learning BCI/fMRI work it is a stronger harmonization than z-scoring features afterwards, and it should leave the within-site differences between autism and controls for the classifier.

I'm replacing the single-atlas model with an ensemble over four parcellations: cc200, aal, ho and dosenbach160. Each atlas gets its own Ledoit-Wolf covariance, tangent-space projection and L2 logistic regression. The final score is the average of the z-scored decision values. Different parcellations draw ROI boundaries differently, so their errors should be partly independent, and Abraham 2017 found that combining atlases helps. I left out cc400 because computing a Riemannian mean on 392×392 matrices would put the run at risk of the time limit. I haven't run this, so there is no Dev score for it yet.

The C=0.001 penalty was fixed by hand. This change picks C for the ~20k tangent-space features (with only ~800 subjects) per training fold instead. It runs a grouped inner 5-fold CV that maximizes AUROC over C ∈ {1e-4 … 3e-2}, using `ctx["groups_train"]` so no subject is split across inner folds. The Riemannian reference and the scaler stay unsupervised and are fitted on the whole training fold. I haven't run this, so there is no Dev score for it yet.

I'm adding a second-stage stacker. The tangent-space logistic regression now produces out-of-fold scores on the training fold through grouped inner CV, and a small L2 logistic regression combines that score with mean_fd (log), age, sex and site one-hot. In the current model, the few known non-imaging predictors (autism is linked to more head motion, and diagnosis rates differ by site) get drowned out among about 20k heavily regularised connectivity features. The round-2 drop after site re-centering suggests site and confound information carries real signal that the model can't currently use.

Every signal is z-scored before the covariance is computed, so the current model never uses regional fluctuation amplitude. Because the data are already band-pass filtered, each ROI's standard deviation is effectively its ALFF. I'm adding the per-ROI log-amplitude profile, centered within each subject to remove site and scanner gain, as a second base learner whose inner-CV out-of-fold score goes into the existing stacker. Regional ALFF/fALFF changes in autism are well reported and should carry information that the connectivity features don't.

Head motion, age and sex leave a known imprint on connectivity and on regional amplitude. Under heavy L2 regularization those confound directions take up a lot of the base learners' capacity. So I'm removing them from the tangent-space and ALFF features with a linear regression on log mean_fd, age and sex, fitted on the training fold only and label-free. The stacker still receives those covariates directly, so any real diagnostic signal in motion, age or site is not lost; it just enters at the stacking stage instead of contaminating the imaging features.

I'm adding a third base learner. It is the same CC200 Ledoit-Wolf → tangent-space → L2 logistic regression pipeline, built on the `filt_global` time series (with global signal regression), and its inner-CV out-of-fold score goes into the existing stacker. Removing the global signal changes the connectivity structure a lot: it shifts the correlation distribution and creates anticorrelations. It also strips out a global, motion-related component, so the GSR view should make errors that partly differ from the no-GSR view. Stacking lets the meta-learner weight the two views rather than averaging them blindly, which is what failed in the round-3 multi-atlas ensemble.

I'm adding a third base learner on the finer CC400 parcellation (~392 ROIs). It uses a Ledoit-Wolf covariance mapped to log-Euclidean tangent space (matrix log of each subject's covariance), followed by an L2 logistic regression, and its inner-CV out-of-fold score goes into the existing stacker. A finer functional parcellation keeps connectivity detail that the 200 parcels average away, and Abraham 2017 found more ROIs help. A full Riemannian mean on 392×392 matrices is too slow, but the log-Euclidean embedding is computed once per subject without labels in `featurize`. That keeps it cheap, and it differs from the CC200 view in both resolution and metric.

I'm adding a fourth base learner that captures dynamic, burst-like co-fluctuation instead of static coupling. For each CC200 edge it takes the log ratio of the mean squared edge time series, mean(z_i² z_j²), to what a stationary Gaussian process with the same correlation would give (1 + 2r²). Following edge-centric FC work (Esfahlani 2020), this measures how much an edge's coupling comes in high-amplitude bursts. It is computed label-free with one matrix product per subject, and it carries fourth-order, time-varying information that every current covariance-based view throws away. Its inner-CV out-of-fold score goes into the existing stacker, so a weak view gets down-weighted. I haven't run it, so there is no Dev score for it yet.

I'm adding a fourth stacked base learner built on CC200 per-ROI temporal autocorrelation: the lag-1 and lag-2 ACF, Fisher-z transformed and centred within each subject. This is a proxy for intrinsic neural timescales, which are reported to be atypical in autism (Watanabe 2019), and none of the current connectivity or amplitude views capture it. Centring within subject removes the global offset that the site-specific TR adds; any remaining scale difference is left to the inner-CV stacker, which can down-weight a weak view. This is untested, so there is no Dev score for it yet.

I'm adding a fifth stacked base learner built on the anatomical Harvard-Oxford (`ho`) atlas: Ledoit-Wolf covariance → log-Euclidean tangent vector → L2 logistic regression. Adding CC400 as a stacked view helped in round 9, and an anatomical parcellation draws ROI boundaries quite differently from the functional CC200/CC400 ones, so its errors should overlap less with the existing views. Its inner-CV out-of-fold score feeds the stacker, which can down-weight it if it turns out weak. I haven't run it, so there's no Dev score yet.

I'm adding a sixth stacked base learner on the Dosenbach-160 atlas: Ledoit-Wolf covariance → log-Euclidean tangent vector → L2 logistic regression, with its inner-CV out-of-fold score fed to the stacker. The CC400 and HO views each helped (rounds 9 and 12). Dosenbach ROIs are small spheres placed from a meta-analysis inside named networks (default-mode, cingulo-opercular, fronto-parietal, sensorimotor, cerebellar), so they sample the brain in a third, different way and should make errors less correlated with the existing views. I haven't run this, so there is no Dev score for it yet.

The two regional time-series views on CC200 both helped: per-ROI amplitude (ALFF proxy) gave +0.0012 and lag-1/2 autocorrelation (intrinsic timescale proxy) gave +0.0056, the largest recent gain. So I'm adding one more stacked base learner that computes the same subject-centred features on the CC400 and Harvard-Oxford parcellations. The finer functional CC400 grid and the anatomical HO boundaries should pick up regional amplitude and timescale differences that CC200 parcels average away or split differently. The values come from time series that `featurize` already loads, and the stacker can down-weight the view if it is weak. I haven't run this, so there's no Dev score for it yet.

This adds a sixth stacked base learner built on graph-theory node strength. For each ROI it takes the mean Fisher-z Pearson correlation with all other ROIs, on CC200 and CC400. The profile is centred within each subject, and the two whole-brain mean connectivity values are added as extra features. Autism is described as having atypical global and regional connectivity strength (under-/over-connectivity hubs). This gives that hypothesis a low-dimensional (~600-feature) summary that is less noisy than the 20k–77k edge tangent vectors. The stacker can down-weight it if it turns out weak. I haven't run it, so there is no Dev score for it yet.

This adds a seventh stacked base learner for directed lead–lag connectivity. For each CC200 pair it takes the antisymmetric part of the lag-1 cross-correlation matrix, (R₁ − R₁ᵀ)/2, on z-scored signals, and divides by its RMS within each subject so site-specific TR doesn't change its scale. Every current view is symmetric (zero-lag covariance, strength) or per-ROI (amplitude, autocorrelation), so none of them sees the order in which regions fluctuate. Mitra et al. reported that this "lag-thread" propagation structure is altered in autism. The ACF timescale view gave the largest recent gain (round 11), which suggests the temporal-ordering information the zero-lag views throw away carries diagnostic signal. I haven't run this, so there is no Dev score for it yet.

This adds a seventh stacked base learner: per-ROI detrended-fluctuation-analysis (DFA) scaling exponents on CC200, a Hurst-exponent proxy, centred within each subject, plus the subject's median exponent. Lai et al. (2010) reported that autism shifts BOLD fluctuations toward randomness (lower Hurst exponent). The current lag-1/2 autocorrelation view gave the largest recent gain, but it only sees short-range memory, while DFA measures scale-free memory across many timescales. It is a low-dimensional (~200-feature), label-free view computed once per subject. I haven't run it, so there's no Dev score yet.

This adds a seventh stacked base learner built on CC200 partial correlations: each subject's precision matrix comes from the Ledoit-Wolf covariance already stored in the features, followed by Fisher-z and an L2 logistic regression. Partial correlation keeps the direct region-to-region couplings and removes the shared, indirect paths. Abraham 2017 ranked it second only to the tangent-space embedding on ABIDE. It weights the small-eigenvalue end of the covariance spectrum quite differently from the current tangent and strength views, so its errors should only partly overlap with theirs. It needs no change to `featurize` and adds little run time; the stacker can down-weight it if it is weak. I haven't run it, so there is no Dev score for it yet.

Autism connectivity differences are known to change with development: hyper-connectivity in children, hypo-connectivity in adolescents and adults (Uddin 2013). ABIDE spans ages 6–64, but every base learner applies one age-independent direction. This change adds, in the stacker only, an interaction of each standardized base-learner score with standardized log-age, so the weight on each view can vary with age. It adds 6 low-dimensional, cheap features that the C=1 stacker regularizes.

Right now the stacker learns from inner-CV out-of-fold base scores, which come from models trained on 80% of the fold, but at test time it receives scores from models refit on 100%. Those refit models have larger decision values under strong L2, so the test-time scores sit on a different scale and the learned balance between the views and the covariates is off. I'm switching to cross-fitted test scores: the average of the inner-fold models' decision values. This puts stacker inputs on the same scale at train and test time, adds a little bagging, and skips the six full refits.
